lesson.menu_title: Presenting to Stakeholders — Holding the Floor
lesson.menu_desc: Standing in front of the board and staying in control of the room: the words of the room, the signposts that guide people through a talk, the turn-taking phrases that keep or hand over the floor, and a full page of speaker notes to read and deliver -- 32 slides

reading.rtitle: Speaker Notes -- Q3 Risk Review for the Board
paras: These are my notes for Thursday. The board has thirty minutes and four other items on the list, so pace is everything. I will open with a one-page overview, not with the model. If I start with the model, I lose the room in the first minute and I never get it back.

The handout goes out before I speak, not during. People read the numbers while I talk, and then nobody listens. So: give it out at the door, ask them to keep it closed, and walk through it together, page by page. I would like to start by explaining what changed since June, then move on to the exposure, and finish with the recommendation.

Two points I want to highlight. First, the limit breach in August: small, closed, already reported. Second, the funding cost, which is the real story. If someone tries to jump in during the first part, I will say: let me finish this point and I will come straight back to you. If I lose the floor early, the second point never happens.

At the end I hand over to Marina for the credit numbers, and she gives the floor back to me for the close. To wrap up, I state the bottom line in one sentence: the desk is inside its limits, but funding costs are eating the margin, and we need a decision on hedging before December.

listenings.text: Hi Sergio, it is Marina. A quick note before Thursday. You have twelve minutes with the board, not twenty, so watch your pace. Please start with the overview, one page, and keep the model out of the first half. Send me the handout tonight and I will print it. When you get to the funding costs, that is the part I want you to highlight, so slow down there. If Claudia jumps in with a question, do not rush your answer and do not lose the floor. Finish the point, then take her question. At the end you hand over to me for the credit numbers, and I will give the floor back to you for the close. Wrap up with one sentence, the bottom line, nothing more. Thanks, and good luck.

Hi Sergio, it is Paulo from the credit desk. One piece of advice about Thursday, from someone who got it wrong last year. Do not walk the board through every slide. They do not want the whole chain, they want the three numbers that changed and what you recommend. I would start by saying where we are, then move on to what changed, and then stop. The other thing is turn-taking. Last year I let a director jump in twice and I never got the floor back, so my last two points died on the page. Say something simple like: let me finish this point and I will come straight back to you. It works, and nobody takes it badly. Good luck on Thursday.

extra_audio.text: First, open with a one-page overview, not with the model. Then signpost the plan and say what you will cover and in what order. Next, walk the room through the numbers that changed. After that, highlight the one point they must remember. Finally, wrap up with the bottom line in a single sentence.
